summary: After a night of prayer on a mountain, Jesus calls His disciples and chooses twelve of them to be with Him and to be sent out as apostles.
key_insight: Before the preaching and the power, Mark names the first purpose of the Twelve: “that they might be with Him.” Jesus was not only recruiting workers; He was gathering companions, and the sending would grow out of time spent with Him.
story: In those days Jesus went out to the mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God. {Lk}

When it was day, He called His disciples to Him, {Lk} those He Himself wanted, and they came to Him. {Mk} From them He chose twelve, whom He also named apostles. {Lk} He appointed them “that they might be with Him and that He might send them out to preach, and to have power to heal sicknesses and to cast out demons.” {Mk}
First came Simon, to whom He gave the name Peter, and Andrew his brother. {Mt} Then James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, whom Jesus named Boanerges, “Sons of Thunder.” {Mk}

Next were Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas, and Matthew the tax collector. {Mt} Then came James the son of Alphaeus; Thaddaeus, {Mk} the man Luke lists as Judas the son of James; {Lk} and Simon the Cananite, whom Luke calls Simon the Zealot. {Lk} Last was Judas Iscariot, “who also became a traitor.” {Lk}
differences: Luke alone says Jesus spent the whole night in prayer before choosing, and that He named the Twelve apostles.
Matthew gives the list later, when Jesus sends the Twelve out (Matthew 10:2–4), and pairs the names two by two.
One name varies: “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus” (Matthew), “Thaddaeus” (Mark), and “Judas the son of James” (Luke, and again in Acts 1:13).
Simon is “the Cananite” in Matthew and Mark and “the Zealot” in Luke and Acts.
Only Mark records the name Boanerges, “Sons of Thunder.” Only Matthew calls Matthew “the tax collector.”

fit.question: Matthew and Mark name Thaddaeus among the Twelve. Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus but list “Judas the son of James.” Do the lists disagree about who the Twelve were?

points.label: More than one name
points.text: Many people in the Gospels went by more than one name: Simon Peter, Levi who is Matthew, Thomas who is called the Twin (John 11:16). Matthew’s own wording, “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus,” already shows that this apostle had more than one name.

points.label: A second Judas
points.text: John mentions “Judas (not Iscariot)” speaking in the upper room (John 14:22), so the Twelve did include a second Judas. After the betrayal, he may well have preferred to be known by another name.

points.label: The lists agree
points.text: All four lists fall into the same three groups of four, each headed by the same man: Peter, Philip and James the son of Alphaeus. Thaddaeus and Judas the son of James stand in the same group.

fit.note: Four lists that agree on eleven names and on their grouping are strong witnesses; the remaining apostle was known by more than one name.
fit.short: Thaddaeus (also called Lebbaeus) and Judas the son of James are one man with more than one name, like Simon Peter or Levi Matthew.

scene.label: Twelve
scene.text: Israel descended from the twelve sons of Jacob and was ordered in twelve tribes. By choosing twelve, Jesus signaled that He was gathering a renewed people of God around Himself. Later He promised the Twelve thrones “judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

scene.label: Apostles
scene.text: The word means people who are sent, messengers who carry the authority of the one who sends them. The Twelve would speak and act in Jesus’ name.

scene.label: A zealot and a tax collector
scene.text: “Cananite” does not mean a man from Canaan. It comes from an Aramaic word for zealous, which Luke translates as “Zealot.” Simon may once have been among those zealous to free Israel from Rome, or simply known for his zeal for the Law. Either way, he served beside Matthew, who had collected taxes, probably for Herod Antipas.

scene.label: Bartholomew
scene.text: The name means son of Tolmai, a family name. John never mentions Bartholomew, the other Gospels never mention Nathanael, and Philip is linked with both, so many think they are the same man (John 1:45).

witnesses.matthew: Saves the list for the moment Jesus sends the Twelve out (10:2–4) and names them in pairs, perhaps the pairs in which they were sent (Mark 6:7). He calls himself “Matthew the tax collector,” the only list that names that past.
witnesses.mark: Stresses Jesus’ initiative: He called “those He Himself wanted.” Mark alone gives the double purpose of the Twelve, to be with Him and to be sent out, and the names Jesus gave: Peter, and Boanerges, “Sons of Thunder.”
witnesses.luke: Shows Jesus praying all night before the choice, as Luke shows Him praying at many turning points. Luke alone says Jesus named them apostles, and he lists them again at the start of Acts (1:13), now without Judas Iscariot.

seeing.reveals: Jesus chose His closest followers after a night in prayer to His Father, and the list includes Judas Iscariot. Nothing about His choosing was careless, and nothing took Him by surprise (John 6:70).
seeing.living: Jesus put a tax collector and a zealot in the same small company, and His call rested on His choice, not on their record. Receive the unlikely people He has called to serve beside you, and spend time with Him before you try to work for Him.
seeing.ponder: Is your work for Jesus growing out of time with Him, or has the work crowded Him out?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus calls whom He wants, first to be with Him, then to be sent.
outline: Sent with His message and authority (14b–15)
Named one by one, Judas included (16–19)
preaching.watch_for: Mark’s words “He Himself wanted” (3:13) put the weight on Jesus’ choice, not on the men’s qualifications. Luke supplies the setting that frames the choice: a whole night of prayer (Luke 6:12).

title: Jesus Chooses the Twelve
